extracted.intended_audience: Title IX coordinators, school and college administrators, investigators, decisionmakers, and legal counsel implementing Title IX grievance procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory preamble guidance on how recipients must run Title IX grievance procedures, focusing on privacy protections, evidentiary rules (what is relevant and what must be excluded), consent/waiver requirements, training, and interactions with due process and First Amendment rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable privacy protections during grievance procedures (§106.45(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must take reasonable steps to protect the privacy of parties and witnesses during the grievance procedures while prohibiting steps that would restrict a party's ability to obtain and present evidence; consult with family members, confidential resources, or advisors; or otherwise prepare for or participate in the grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privacy measures should be tailored by recipients to particular circumstances (including language assistance) and must balance privacy with fairness; overly restrictive measures (e.g., those that prevent obtaining evidence or consulting advisors) are prohibited. The Department replaced the phrases “prepare for a hearing, if one is offered” and “otherwise defend their interests” with “otherwise prepare for or participate in the grievance procedures” to clarify scope. Recipients must inform parties of grievance procedures (see §§106.44(f)(1)(iii), 106.45(c)(1)(i)).

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment considerations in privacy protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must be mindful of First Amendment rights when taking reasonable steps to protect privacy under §106.45(b)(5); nothing in the Title IX regulations requires restricting rights protected by the First Amendment (§106.6(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable privacy steps may include prohibiting identification of parties/witnesses while proceedings are ongoing and may, depending on circumstances and consistent with the First Amendment, limit widespread social media or media disclosures of personally identifiable information. The Department rejects the idea that §106.45(b)(5) invites gag orders and declines a categorical prohibition on criticizing a recipient's handling of complaints, but also clarifies that limits consistent with the First Amendment are permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evaluation of all evidence that is relevant (§106.45(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient's grievance procedures must require an objective evaluation of all evidence that is relevant (as defined in §106.2: “related to the allegations of sex discrimination” and useful to determining whether the alleged sex discrimination occurred), excluding evidence that is impermissible under §106.45(b)(7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department retained the ordinary meaning of “relevant” and cross-references §106.2. Investigators/decisionmakers must objectively evaluate inculpatory and exculpatory evidence; parties may raise concerns about relevance as part of their opportunity to respond (§§106.45(f)(4)(ii), 106.46(e)(6)(ii)). Training on the meaning/application of relevance is required (§106.8(d)(2)(iv)), and erroneous relevance determinations that affected outcome may be appealed (§106.46(i)(1)(i)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of impermissible evidence regardless of relevance (§106.45(b)(7))
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of evidence (and questions seeking that evidence) must not be accessed, considered, disclosed, or otherwise used in grievance procedures even if they are relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three categories of impermissible evidence mirror prohibitions in the 2020 amendments and include particularly sensitive or legally protected materials (e.g., medical records, prior sexual conduct, privileged communications). Recipients may access such evidence only for the narrow purpose of determining whether an exception under §106.45(b)(7)(i)–(iii) applies. The Department emphasizes sensitivity of these materials and the policy reasons for exclusion (protecting privacy, avoiding chilling participation, preventing prejudice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of privileged evidence and evidence provided to confidential employees (§106.45(b)(7)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence protected by a Federal or State recognized privilege and evidence provided to a confidential employee must be excluded unless the person to whom the privilege or confidentiality is owed voluntarily waives the privilege or confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The waiver must be voluntary, but the Department removed a requirement that waiver follow a jurisdiction's specific manner; recipients have discretion to specify waiver manner (e.g., written) unless an existing legal waiver standard applies. If the same information is available from non-confidential sources, it may be accessed and used. Title IX coordinators are required to notify parties about what evidence/questions are impermissible (see §§106.44(f)(1)(iii), 106.45(c)(1)(i)). The Department declined to require recipients to advise parties to consult counsel regarding privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of records made or maintained in connection with treatment (§106.45(b)(7)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Records made or maintained by a physician, psychologist, or other recognized professional or paraprofessional in connection with the provision of treatment to a party or witness must not be accessed, considered, disclosed, or otherwise used in grievance procedures unless the recipient obtains that party's or witness's voluntary, written consent for use in the grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protection extends to witnesses and includes student IEPs and Section 504 plans. The Department declined to create an exception (e.g., for physical injury) and maintained that treatment records are among the most sensitive documents. Recipients must still comply with other applicable laws (FERPA, State law) and should be mindful of HIPAA interaction though Title IX does not enforce HIPAA. The Department noted recipients may choose to allow students access to treatment records prior to consent but are not required to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of evidence about complainant's sexual interests or prior sexual conduct (§106.45(b)(7)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence and questions regarding a complainant's sexual interests or prior sexual conduct are presumptively excluded; prior sexual conduct between the parties does not prove or imply consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two narrow exceptions exist but the Department rejected applying an ordinary relevance standard or importing criminal Rule 412 exceptions; the exclusion applies across recipients (including elementary/secondary settings). Parties may argue during their opportunity to respond why evidence should not be excluded. The Department declined to extend these protections to respondents, and maintained that importing complex criminal evidentiary rules could deter non-lawyers from serving as decisionmakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow exception permitting recipient to access impermissible evidence to determine applicability of exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may access or consider impermissible evidence (and questions seeking that evidence) only for the narrow purpose of determining whether an exception in §106.45(b)(7)(i) through (iii) applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outside that narrow purpose, impermissible evidence must not be accessed, considered, disclosed, or otherwise used. Decisionmakers may consider whether a party's partial withholding of consent is reasonable when assessing credibility and responsibility (e.g., redaction, privilege, legal protection, or lack of access to portions of a document).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice, opportunity to respond, and appeal related to relevance and impermissible evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must be informed of the grievance procedures (including what evidence is impermissible) and have procedural opportunities to contest relevance or assert that evidence should not be excluded; certain erroneous relevance determinations that affected outcome may be appealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice obligations arise under §§106.44(f)(1)(iii) and 106.45(c)(1)(i). Parties may raise relevance concerns as part of their reasonable opportunity to respond (§§106.45(f)(4)(ii), 106.46(e)(6)(ii)), recipients may allow other opportunities to contest relevance (§106.45(j)), and appeals are available under §106.46(i)(1)(i) for outcome-affecting erroneous relevance determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirements on relevance and impermissible evidence (§106.8(d)(2) / §106.8(d)(2)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: All investigators, decisionmakers, and other persons responsible for implementing the grievance procedures must receive training on the meaning and application of the term “relevant” and on the types of evidence that are impermissible regardless of relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required training is expected to assist recipients (including elementary and secondary schools) in applying exclusions such as §106.45(b)(7)(iii) and in making appropriate relevance determinations. The training supports consistent, impartial, and fair application of the evidentiary rules.
